question:
Patient note:
A 38-year-old man was brought to the ambulatory evaluation bay early this morning after observing that the mid-portion of his left calf “ballooned” over the prior thirty-six hours while his right leg remained unchanged. Three weeks ago he sustained a nondisplaced distal fibular fracture while playing recreational basketball; emergency clinicians applied a below-knee fiberglass cast that immobilized the ankle in neutral, and he was given crutches with non-weight-bearing instructions. He returned to the orthopedic clinic eight days ago, at which time interval radiographs were satisfactory; the cast, however, was left in place because of mild tenderness over the fracture site, and he has continued to keep the limb essentially fixed except for brief heel-touch balancing when showering. He denies any other external brace or splint, and reports that he can voluntarily move the knee and hip without weakness, numbness, or back pain. Aside from a remote appendectomy in adolescence he has undergone no operations, invasive procedures, or hospitalizations, and he has never been treated for malignancy, inflammatory bowel disease, nephrotic syndrome, or heart failure. Medications are limited to over-the-counter ibuprofen 400 mg taken twice daily for fracture soreness and a daily multivitamin; he does not use estrogen preparations, systemic corticosteroids, erythropoiesis-stimulating agents, or anticoagulants. There is no personal or first-degree family history of venous thromboembolism, premature coronary disease, or known thrombophilia. He has never smoked, drinks two craft beers on weekend evenings, and denies recreational drug use. Yesterday at work—he is a graphic designer who sits for prolonged periods but normally walks to a café several blocks away for lunch—he noticed his left cargo pant leg felt snug. Upon returning home he measured both calves with a tailor’s tape: at a point he estimated to be about a handbreadth below the kneecap the left side was nearly four centimeters larger than the right; the cast limited more distal assessment. This morning the calf felt tight when he lowered the limb from the bed, prompting evaluation. He denies antecedent fever, chills, night sweats, rash, insect bite, trauma beyond the original fracture, groin mass, abdominal pain, flank pain, dysuria, cough, pleuritic chest discomfort, palpitations, or light-headedness. On arrival—before receiving any analgesic, intravenous fluid, or antithrombotic agent—he sat upright with the injured leg elevated on a pillow, conversing comfortably. Vital signs were temperature 36.7 °C, blood pressure 124/78 mm Hg, heart rate 84 beats min⁻¹ regular, respiratory rate 14 breaths min⁻¹, and oxygen saturation 98 % on ambient air. Cardiac examination revealed a crisp S₁ and S₂ without murmurs, rubs, or gallops; lungs were clear to auscultation throughout. The abdomen was flat, soft, and non-tender with normal bowel sounds. Inspection of the lower extremities showed the fiberglass cast extending from just distal to the tibial tuberosity to the metatarsal heads; the padding could be retracted sufficiently at the proximal aperture to allow circumference measurement exactly 10 cm distal to the inferior pole of the patella: 42.3 cm on the left versus 38.7 cm on the right, a 3.6-cm discrepancy. Fifteen centimeters above the patella both thighs measured 55.1 cm. Because the cast covered the malleolar region and foot, comparison there was deferred. The proximal calf skin visible at the cast opening was taut and glistening but retained a uniform pink hue, matched contralateral temperature to the dorsum of the examiner’s hand, and displayed intact hair follicles without induration, discoloration, dermatitis, or serpiginous dilated veins. Gentle but firm palpation along the expected course of the common femoral vein beneath the inguinal ligament, through the adductor canal, and into the popliteal fossa provoked no pinpoint pain; the patient reported only a deep sense of fullness when diffuse pressure was applied to the posterior compartment through the cast window. No palpable cord, crepitus, fluctuance, or popliteal mass was detected, and passive ankle dorsiflexion within the cast elicited a stretching sensation rather than sharp discomfort. Hip and knee ranges of motion were full and pain-free; distal sensation was intact to light touch in all toes accessed through the cast window, capillary refill was <2 s, and dorsalis pedis pulse on the casted side was 2 + by Doppler, symmetric with the contralateral limb. There was no inguinal or popliteal lymphadenopathy. A twelve-lead electrocardiogram obtained prior to phlebotomy displayed normal sinus rhythm at 82 beats min⁻¹ with no ST-T abnormalities. Point-of-care laboratory studies drawn before any imaging or medication showed hemoglobin 14.1 g dL⁻¹, platelet count 246 × 10⁹ L⁻¹, white blood cell count 6.2 × 10⁹ L⁻¹, serum sodium 140 mmol L⁻¹, potassium 4.3 mmol L⁻¹, bicarbonate 25 mmol L⁻¹, blood urea nitrogen 12 mg dL⁻¹, creatinine 0.92 mg dL⁻¹, alanine aminotransferase 23 U L⁻¹, aspartate aminotransferase 21 U L⁻¹, international normalized ratio 1.0, and activated partial thromboplastin time 28 s. Repeat ankle radiographs confirmed the fracture remained well aligned without periosteal reaction or soft-tissue gas. No cellulitis, ruptured Baker cyst, gastrocnemius tear, lymphatic obstruction, cardiac failure, renal insufficiency, or volume overload was evident on clinical examination to offer a more compelling explanation for the abrupt unilateral calf enlargement occurring while the limb has been immobilized in a cast, so comprehensive duplex ultrasonography from the common femoral vein through the infrapopliteal segments has been requested on an expedited basis while the patient remains hemodynamically stable and untreated in observation with the leg elevated at heart level.

Question: What is the patient's score of Wells' criteria for Deep Vein Thrombosis? You should use the patient's medical values and health status when they were first admitted to the hospital prior to any treatment.
solution:
Apply the Wells DVT score to the pretreatment examination. Each positive risk or examination criterion adds 1 point; an alternative diagnosis at least as likely as DVT subtracts 2.
- Recent lower-limb cast immobilization: +1.
- Calf swelling at least 3 cm greater than the asymptomatic side: 42.3 − 38.7 = 3.6 cm, so +1.
- Active cancer, prior DVT, recent qualifying bed rest or major surgery, localized deep venous tenderness, entire-leg swelling, unilateral pitting edema, and nonvaricose collateral superficial veins: none documented, 0 each. Calf fullness alone does not establish focal tenderness or pitting edema.
- No alternative diagnosis judged at least as likely as DVT: no deduction.
Sum: 1 + 1 = 2.
Final answer: 2
